Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3

src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 5
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.
Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
 Mandatory 13
File
oracle-init/create-user.sh

Explanation

The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component. Without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java web application with server-rendered gallery pages, a multipart upload API, and database-backed image delivery. These diagrams describe repository-defined behavior and Docker Compose topology, not a verified live deployment; secret values are omitted.

Application Architecture

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the runtime system of record: the photos entity contains UUID identifiers, filenames, timestamps, dimensions and a photo_data BLOB (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-97). Uploads save bytes to the database, not an upload directory; stored filenames and file paths remain compatibility metadata (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-124,160-174). Image responses read those bytes through the service (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-83). Compose persists database files in oracle_data and mounts initialization scripts (docker-compose.yml:12-14). Both application profiles configure Hibernate schema creation at startup, so a persistent database volume does not imply schema/data preservation across application restarts (src/main/resources/application.properties:17-21; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:13-17).

The browser fetches Bootstrap from jsDelivr, rather than the backend calling a business API (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7,124). No runtime cache, message broker or object-storage integration is evident in the inspected application sources and dependencies. H2 is test-scoped, not the runtime database (pom.xml:88-93). Database and administrator passwords are externally supplied; no secret values are reproduced here (docker-compose.yml:30-36; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:34-42).

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Layered monolith with constructor injection: controllers depend on the PhotoService interface; its implementation receives PhotoRepository and upload configuration. Business operations use Spring transactions, with read-only retrieval methods (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-32; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-55).
  • Database-centric image persistence: metadata and BLOBs share one entity; the repository uses Oracle-specific SQL, including ROWNUM, NVL and TO_CHAR, rather than a database-neutral query layer (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-79; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:34-71).
  • Public reads, authenticated mutations: HTTP Basic protects upload and delete POST routes; other requests are permitted. Credentials are BCrypt-encoded in memory, sessions are stateless, and CSRF protection is explicitly disabled (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-61). This describes configuration, not a security assurance.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicit HTTP handlers expose gallery/detail pages, multipart upload, deletion, and binary photo retrieval. Browser requests and backend operations are request/response based; no message-driven service contracts were found.

oracle-db1521, published as 1521InfrastructureThird-party gvenzl/oracle-free container providing the application's database; no application HTTP API.

No Kubernetes, Helm, or IaC service definitions were found in the inspected conventional deployment directories.

API Endpoints Inventory

All handlers belong to photoalbum-java-app. Paths are unversioned; no header/query version selection or controller-level base API prefix is implemented.

Service / controllerMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
Application / HomeControllerGET/No required parametersNormally 200 HTML, template index; model contains List and a timestamp. A caught retrieval exception produces the same page with an empty photo list.
Application / HomeControllerPOST/uploadmultipart/form-data, required repeated part files bound to List; HTTP Basic authentication200 JSON Map containing aggregate success and per-file results, including when all files fail at service level. Explicit empty-list guard returns 400 JSON; missing required part is rejected by framework binding. Unauthenticated/invalid credentials: 401. Unhandled service/transaction exceptions may produce framework 5xx responses.
Application / DetailControllerGET/detail/{id}Path id: StringNormally 200 HTML, template detail, with Photo and optional neighboring photo IDs. Missing photo, blank ID, or caught exception returns redirect:/ (normally 302), not a 404 JSON response.
Application / DetailControllerPOST/detail/{id}/deletePath id: String; no body DTO; HTTP Basic authenticationredirect:/ (normally 302), with success/error flash attribute, including missing photo or caught deletion error. Unauthenticated/invalid credentials: 401.
Application / PhotoFileControllerGET/photo/{id}Path id: String; browser may append _t as an ignored cache-busting query value200 raw image bytes as ResponseEntity / ByteArrayResource; MIME type taken from stored metadata. 404 for blank/missing ID or absent bytes; 500 for caught exceptions.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-49,55-98; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:17-18,32-58,64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:22-23,37-86; authentication rules in src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:45-61; browser cache-busting in src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:176-179.

Upload response semantics: the JSON envelope uses success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads; the explicit 400 guard instead uses success and error. success means at least one photo was added to uploadedPhotos, not that every supplied file succeeded. A successful save is followed by another lookup; if that lookup returns empty, that file appears in neither result list. Service-level file rejection is represented in failedUploads, not by a per-file HTTP status (HomeController.java:62-97, at the controller path above). Framework multipart limits can reject requests before this handler; no application-specific oversize-error mapping was found.

Binary response headers: Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size are explicitly emitted (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:74-83). Upload metadata's compatibility filePath is not the binary retrieval contract; clients use /photo/{id} (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-115,160-166; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:176-179).

Static assets are framework-served resources rather than additional controller APIs; the gallery references /css/site.css and /js/upload.js (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:8,124-125). No separate list/detail JSON API, pagination endpoint, PUT/PATCH handler, or HTTP DELETE handler was found; deletion uses POST.

No gateway-level aggregation DTOs, immutable records, or Lombok value classes were found. For entity fields and persistence structure, see the companion data-architecture.md; individual validation rules belong in business-workflows.md.

JSON is provided through the Spring Boot JSON starter and normal Spring MVC message conversion; upload uses @ResponseBody and ResponseEntity, while page handlers return template names. No custom Jackson configuration or serializers were found in the inspected Java/configuration files. Consumers parse upload JSON and construct dates from its timestamp metadata (pom.xml:75-79; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-57,79; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:110-120,161-170). No OpenAPI/Swagger documents or annotations, protobuf schemas, or GraphQL schemas were found in the inspected application/build files.

Communication Patterns

  • Browser to application: same-origin HTTP page navigation, multipart upload through fetch, and binary image requests. JavaScript uses async/await, but this is asynchronous browser execution of an ordinary request/response HTTP exchange, not queue-based messaging. The delete operation is an HTML form POST (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:90-106; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59,67-70).
  • Inside the application: controllers call PhotoService synchronously; PhotoServiceImpl calls PhotoRepository synchronously under Spring transactions. Repository access uses JPA/JDBC, not a second REST service (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-31,40,68-72; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-47,53-75,172-185; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-16).
  • External dependency: the configured database target uses the Compose service hostname oracle-db on port 1521; this is network/DNS name resolution, not Eureka/Consul registration. No Feign, RestTemplate, WebClient, gRPC clients, discovery registry, client-side load balancing, API gateway, or cross-service aggregation was found. Detail-page composition combines photo data with neighboring IDs within the same service (src/main/resources/application.properties:12,15; docker-compose.yml:3,32,39-43; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-54).
  • Other browser traffic: page templates reference Bootstrap CSS/JavaScript from an external HTTPS CDN. These are browser asset dependencies, not backend business-service calls (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7,124; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:7,147).
  • Async messaging: no message broker, pub/sub, queue client, or asynchronous backend event contract was found in pom.xml:30-101 or the inspected application sources.
  • Retries, timeouts, isolation: no application-defined HTTP/JDBC request timeout, retry policy, circuit breaker, bulkhead, or retry fallback was found. The upload browser call does not set an abort timeout or retry (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:102-132); repository operations have no explicit retry wrapper (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:53-75,172-217). Framework/driver defaults are not documented timeout guarantees. Compose's process restart policy is not a request retry (docker-compose.yml:44).
  • Error/fallback contract: gallery lookup errors render an empty gallery; detail errors redirect home; binary retrieval returns 404/500; delete errors redirect with a flash message; upload catches many per-file errors and returns failed outcomes. These are local error-handling paths, not circuit-breaker fallbacks. Transaction-commit failures can still escape the upload service call because the controller has no surrounding catch (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-49,68-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-58,64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-29,181-192).
  • Availability dependencies: Compose starts the application after database readiness; required externally supplied database and administrator credentials also affect successful startup. Full startup/configuration details belong in configuration-inventory.md (docker-compose.yml:30-41; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-42). No secret values are reproduced here.
  • API security: stateless HTTP Basic protects POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete; anonymous or invalidly authenticated callers receive the framework Basic challenge/401. All other requests are permitted. The configured user is assigned an admin role, but route rules check authentication only, not roles or ownership. CSRF is explicitly disabled; no JWT/OAuth flow, method-level authorization, or custom CORS policy was found (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-61). The upload JavaScript supplies no explicit authorization header or login flow; it relies on browser authentication behavior and displays a generic error for non-2xx results (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:102-131).
  • Transport: no application HTTPS listener, TLS enforcement, or database TLS configuration was found in the supplied runtime settings. Port 8080 is exposed directly in Compose; any production TLS termination outside this repository is unverified (src/main/resources/application.properties:1-15; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:1-6,25; docker-compose.yml:37-38). External CDN URLs use HTTPS, which does not establish TLS for the application's API.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Operator environment → Compose validation → containers: required Oracle, application-schema and admin passwords must be supplied before Compose can resolve the service definitions (docker-compose.yml:7-9,34-36).
  2. Oracle image initialization → mounted scripts: Compose mounts ./oracle-init at /container-entrypoint-initdb.d; the shell script requires Oracle credentials and sleeps 30 seconds before SQL execution (docker-compose.yml:12-14; oracle-init/create-user.sh:11-22). SQL grant and verification files assume the fixed photoalbum account even when APP_USER is overridden (oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:15-30; oracle-init/02-verify-user.sql:4-12).
  3. Application → waits for → healthy Oracle: depends_on.condition=service_healthy; Oracle's image-provided healthcheck.sh runs every 30 seconds, timeout 10 seconds, retries 15, start period 180 seconds (docker-compose.yml:17-22,39-41). oracle-init/healthcheck.sql:1-3 exists, but Compose does not directly reference it.
  4. Spring context → required external properties: database and admin passwords must resolve before their consumers initialize (src/main/resources/application.properties:10-14; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:34-42). No application readiness/liveness probe, explicit datasource retry policy, or application startup timeout is declared in Compose.
  5. Separate Azure provisioning order: existing Azure CLI login/account → resource group → ACR → AKS → ACR attachment → PostgreSQL server → database → firewall rules → FQDN lookup → fixed 30-second sleep → SQL user/grants → root .env output (azure-setup.ps1:43-299). This provisions resources; it does not establish a deployed application startup chain.

The Oracle shell script targets service XE, whereas the application uses FREEPDB1; this is an initialization/configuration mismatch to verify, not evidence that both are available (oracle-init/create-user.sh:22; docker-compose.yml:32). README's Oracle XE image/service description also differs from Compose's Oracle Free image (README.md:65-70; docker-compose.yml:2-4).

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  • Local containers: copy .env.example to .env, replace every password placeholder with an operator-supplied value, then start Compose (README.md:40-46; .env.example:1-17). Compose rejects absent/empty passwords, passes the schema secret to both services and the admin secret only to the application (docker-compose.yml:7-9,30-36). Oracle initialization consumes environment credentials; SQL grants are schema-scoped rather than DBA (oracle-init/create-user.sh:11-35; oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:7-30).
  • Application binding: datasource placeholders and Spring's environment property binding supply credentials. SecurityConfig BCrypt-encodes the injected admin password for its in-memory user; this is password hashing, not encryption of the source environment or .env (src/main/resources/application.properties:10-15; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-42).
  • Azure provisioning: uses the already-authenticated Azure CLI account; no explicit service-principal login or application managed-identity secret access is defined (azure-setup.ps1:43-50). Passwords come from environment variables or a cryptographic RNG with default length 24 (azure-setup.ps1:12-23,35-41). They are passed to Azure CLI provisioning/SQL commands; only the app password is persisted as POSTGRES_PASSWORD in root .env (azure-setup.ps1:117-127,206-212,274-299). The script enables ACR administrator access and attaches ACR to AKS, but defines no Key Vault/Secret resource binding (azure-setup.ps1:69-74,99-105).
  • Storage/access boundaries: .env is ignored by Git, not encrypted; filesystem access restrictions and rotation are not configured by these scripts (.gitignore:201-204; azure-setup.ps1:299). No Jasypt, sealed secrets, DPAPI, Vault, or Key Vault provisioning flow was found. Workflow GitHub tokens remain separate repository-automation credentials.

This inventory is based on static evidence only; no tests, builds, dependency resolution, deployments, or live configuration checks were performed.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared collection of photographs, inspect individual images, and navigate by upload time. Authenticated users can add photographs in batches and remove photographs from the collection.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo CollectionIndependently managed photograph combining image content with information needed for display and chronological navigation.No owner, album, or other domain-entity association is modeled; previous and next photos are derived from upload times.
UploadResult (operation result, not a persisted entity)PhotoService / Upload ProcessingPer-file acceptance or rejection outcome used to assemble batch feedback.References a successfully created Photo or identifies a rejected input file and reason.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-29; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:225-237.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application with one business service, not independently deployed domain services. The controller roles below are internal presentation boundaries, not separate sources of truth.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplPhoto collection, upload acceptance, chronological browsing, removalPhoto; produces UploadResultPhotoRepository and the photo database; image-header inspection
HomeControllerGallery and batch-upload orchestrationNone; composes Photo summaries and upload outcomesInternal PhotoService
DetailControllerIndividual viewing, navigation, deletion feedbackNone; composes current and adjacent PhotosInternal PhotoService
PhotoFileControllerImage deliveryNone; serves content from PhotoInternal PhotoService

The Photo repository is the collection's source of truth. These roles exchange in-process calls and photo identifiers, not events or inter-service requests. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-48,160-174,199-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-40,68-83; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:23-27,39-52; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-32,46-69.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch and publish accepted photos

  1. A user selects or drops files. The browser applies the Upload eligibility checks and submits eligible files to POST /upload; the security boundary requires authentication.
  2. HomeController applies Batch acceptance, then calls PhotoService once per file, sequentially.
  3. PhotoService applies Upload eligibility and Image dimension handling, generates a compatibility filename, reads content, and creates a Photo with its upload identity and time.
  4. The service saves the Photo with its content. Rejected files or handled read/save failures produce a failed UploadResult rather than a successful photo.
  5. For each successful result, HomeController rereads the Photo by identifier and assembles a display summary. It separates summaries from rejected-file reasons under Batch outcome composition.
  6. The browser displays success/error feedback and prepends accepted photos to the gallery. Rendering uses the real photo-serving URL, not the compatibility upload path.

There is no external service orchestration or all-or-nothing batch transaction. Save/commit or subsequent reread exceptions can still abort the request rather than produce a complete per-file response; successful service return is not a guarantee that every later step succeeds.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-131,154-179; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:45-60; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:82-192.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and inspect neighboring photos

  1. A visitor opens GET /. The application retrieves photos newest first and renders gallery cards.
  2. If collection retrieval fails, HomeController supplies an empty collection; visitors see the same empty-gallery presentation used when no photos exist.
  3. Opening GET /detail/{id} retrieves the chosen Photo and composes older/newer navigation using Chronological navigation. Invalid, missing, or failed lookups redirect to the gallery.
  4. The browser separately requests GET /photo/{id} for the image content. The serving controller applies Image availability and returns image bytes or an error; it does not substitute a default image.
  5. The detail view displays available image dimensions and human-readable file size; navigation buttons appear only when a corresponding neighbor exists.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-49; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:22-56; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:82-108; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:67-93,114-125.

Workflow 3: Remove a photograph and return to the gallery

  1. The detail page asks for browser confirmation before submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete; authentication is required by the security boundary.
  2. PhotoService retrieves the Photo. If present, it deletes the record containing the image content; no separate file deletion is performed.
  3. A missing Photo yields a not-found outcome. A repository exception becomes a service exception.
  4. DetailController converts the outcome into success, not-found, or failure flash feedback and redirects to the gallery. There is no soft-delete or recovery workflow.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:54-60; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:199-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78.

No scheduled, message-driven, or business-state initialization entry point was found in the Java source. The application entry point only starts the application (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14). Month filtering, pagination, and statistics repository methods have no invocation in the inspected business service/controllers, so they are not presented as active user workflows (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:58-100).

Cross-Service Data Flows

There is no gateway aggregation, remote business service, message exchange, or circuit breaker in these workflows. Composition happens inside the application:

  • Upload composition: per-file UploadResult supplies a photo identifier; HomeController rereads that Photo and maps it to a gallery summary. A successful result whose reread returns empty contributes neither a summary nor a failed-file entry (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-95).
  • Detail composition: DetailController combines the current Photo with identifiers derived from older/newer photo queries; all data comes from the same collection (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:39-52).
  • Content delivery: gallery/detail markup points the browser at the image-serving controller, which retrieves content from the same Photo. The /uploads/ path produced during upload is compatibility metadata, not the serving route (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-115,160-174; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:94-95; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:46-83).

Business-relevant degradation is local: collection errors appear as an empty gallery, detail errors redirect home, image-content failures return not-found/server-error, and handled per-file upload errors allow remaining files to be attempted. There is no remote fallback or compensating process (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:44-48,68-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:34-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:48-61,84-86).

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Acceptance and validation

  • Upload eligibility: browser accepts JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP and limits each file to 10 MiB. Server checks the lowercased declared content type against the configured allowlist, then the configured size limit, then rejects zero-length content. Current configuration matches those formats and the 10 MiB service limit. These are declared MIME checks, not proof that content matches its declared format (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:65-79; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:86-110; src/main/resources/application.properties:24-29).
  • Image dimension handling: header inspection rejects images exceeding 40,000,000 pixels when dimensions can be read. An I/O failure rejects the upload, but unavailable readers or other dimension-extraction failures allow processing without dimensions. Full image decoding is not required for acceptance (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:34-35,122-158).
  • Batch acceptance: no files produces a bad-request response. The configuration declares a ten-files-per-upload setting, but the inspected controller and browser do not enforce that count; the multipart request-size limit is 50 MB (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:62-69; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-106; src/main/resources/application.properties:24-30).
  • Entity validation declarations: original and stored filenames must be nonblank and at most 255 characters; compatibility path at most 500; MIME type nonblank and at most 50; file size required and positive; upload time required. These are model annotations, not a separate controller validation pass. Content and dimensions have no equivalent required-value validation annotation (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:31-91).

Outcomes, lifecycle, and derived behavior

  • Batch outcome composition: a nonempty submitted batch returns an OK response after normal completion, even if every per-file result fails. Top-level success means at least one saved Photo was reread and included in the response, not that every input succeeded (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-97).
  • Photo lifecycle: input becomes either rejected or a newly stored Photo; a stored Photo can later be physically deleted. There are no moderation, edit, approval, or soft-delete states. New Photos receive generated identities and the current upload time; there is no content-based deduplication check in upload (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:93-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-115,160-174,199-213).
  • Chronological navigation: gallery order is descending upload time. Previous is the first strictly older result ordered newest first; next is the first strictly newer result ordered oldest first. Equal timestamps are excluded from both neighbor searches, and no tie-breaker is specified (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:22-56; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:225-237).
  • Image availability: blank identifiers, absent Photos, and missing/empty content return not-found; other serving exceptions return server-error. No generated thumbnail or replacement image is created (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86).
  • Display derivations: file size is formatted in bytes/KB/MB on the detail page; dimensions are displayed only when both are present. Newly uploaded gallery cards are prepended as each returned summary is processed; full-page ordering comes from the repository (src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:114-125; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:154-174,195-196; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:22-27).

Cross-cutting controls

  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl has a class-level transaction boundary; collection, identifier, and neighbor reads explicitly use read-only transactions. The controller is not transactional, so separate upload calls are separate transaction invocations; no batch-wide rollback or saga is implemented. Catching a save exception does not guarantee that transaction completion will succeed (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-29,53-75,173-190,223-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-97).
  • Error handling: upload uses per-file result messages for handled validation, read, save, and unexpected exceptions. Read/delete service failures become runtime exceptions; controllers map these to the workflow-specific degradation described above. No automatic retry, dead-letter handling, or compensation is present in these paths (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:55-75,150-190,199-217).
  • Authorization: upload and delete require an authenticated caller; other requests are permitted publicly. An in-memory account is assigned an administrator role, but route checks require authentication rather than checking that role or photo ownership. Credentials are configuration-supplied; secret values are intentionally omitted. The security configuration uses stateless Basic authentication and disables CSRF (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-60).
  • Audit/logging: upload acceptance/rejection, retrieval failures, and deletion outcomes are logged. Image delivery also logs filenames, content sizes, and a short byte preview; these are operational logs, not a dedicated actor-linked business audit trail (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:91-101,179-189,203-216; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:45-72).

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 is a legacy release outside its original open-source support window; commercial support availability is not established here (pom.xml:8-13). The build targets Java 8 (pom.xml:23-26), so migration to Spring Boot 3 or later requires a newer Java baseline and review of Jakarta namespace compatibility. Commons IO is pinned to the older 2.11.0 release (pom.xml:69-73); review current supported versions and security advisories before retaining it. Oracle and H2 compatibility cannot be assessed precisely until their managed versions are resolved. These are compatibility observations, not a vulnerability scan.

Notable Observations

  • Versions are centralized through the Spring Boot parent except for the explicit Commons IO pin; no local dependency-management override or imported BOM is declared (pom.xml:8-13,30-101).
  • The JSON starter is separately declared alongside the Web starter. Potential transitive overlap should be checked with a resolved dependency tree; despite its “Image processing” comment, the declared artifact is a JSON starter, not an image-processing library (pom.xml:31-35,75-79).
  • DevTools is optional but has default compile scope, not test scope; it is therefore included in the non-test count (pom.xml:95-100).
  • The build declares org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-maven-plugin without an explicit version. This is build tooling, excluded from library counts and the diagram (pom.xml:103-109).

Data Ownership Boundaries

The inspected application has one repository and one configured datasource per active environment, with no database-per-service split, separate read model, or tenant/owner partition in Photo. Reads and writes use the same entity/table through PhotoServiceImpl; there is no CQRS persistence separation or cross-service data aggregation in the inspected persistence code (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-100; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:37-47,53-71,172-174,198-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-91).

Both image bytes and metadata belong to the photo persistence boundary. Compatibility filenames/paths do not designate an independently authoritative filesystem or blob store: upload reads bytes into the entity, and image delivery reads those bytes back (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-124,160-174; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:53-69). Test storage is an in-memory H2 alternative, not an additional production data owner (src/test/resources/application-test.properties:1-9).

Database credentials are externalized, not entity fields; secret values are omitted from this report. Infrastructure-level encryption and actual uploaded-content sensitivity cannot be verified from these source files.
